entry.title: It All Starts With a Spreadsheet
entry.content:
From What's Next, Richmond?

Subscribe now

1. From Car-Centric to Car-Lite Living

I sold my personal car and switched to biking to work nearly 2 years ago.

It started as somewhat of a fluke involving a devious plan to sell my car when the value was high on used cars, dump the money into cryptocurrency, then buy a new car once the prices had dropped again, making a handsome profit. I could always use my wife’s car in the mean time, and it was guaranteed money, right?

Falling to the same fate of the multitude of other cryptocurrency “investors,” I watched my “diversified” crypto holdings drop to 25% of their original value. The used car market also didn’t recede in the way I had anticipated. Needless to say, my master plan had flopped.

Flash forward to August of 2022, I was waving goodbye to my wife and 4 month old daughter and beginning my first bike ride to work post paternity leave.

As I grew comfortable biking to more places that I once drove to, I also began to learn the GRTC bus system in Richmond. Riding the bus has a sort of charm to it for me, and it also has the added bonus that my daughter can ride in my lap. Over time I grew to feel that riding the bus was a community experience that I could share with my daughter, whereas shoving her into the back of the car every time I wanted to go somewhere felt cumbersome and lonely.

In August of 2023 my daughter started daycare. Though initially resistant to the idea, my very patient wife eventually agreed to allow me to continue to bike to work with my daughter sitting up front in her yepp mini bike seat. I take the protected bike lanes downtown to drop her off at school then continue on with my commute. This year I haven’t driven her into a day care a single time (though we do occasionally take the bus to daycare and then I catch a scooter into work from there).

I’ve found a sense of both peace and of adventure in living a car-lite life. The peace may be hard to convince daily drivers of. It wasn’t until I had gone without driving regularly for a while until I realized just how much stress my body was carrying while driving (The fact that road rage is so common makes me believe that I’m not the only person who finds driving stressful). The sense of adventure comes from navigating my city in a way that takes a little more creativity at times, but with the comfort of knowing that my decisions are having a better impact on the environment and encourage me to engage with my community at large.

2. Combative Civic Engagement

The combination of biking daily for a year and having a daughter led me to develop new opinions about the dangers of traffic. When people speed on neighborhood streets or don’t look before blowing into intersections they could (and frequently do) kill a pedestrian or cyclist. I came to believe that the built environment of the city itself was responsible for these behaviors. Reckless drivers aren’t to blame, but rather wide streets and intersections encourage normal drivers to behave recklessly.

With this new belief I began to email with city officials about car accidents, designs, and complaints about the way things were built in the city.

To their credit they largely did respond to my inquiries and complaints. I had separate correspondences with a city council rep, the rep’s liaison, and an engineer from the city, all of whom would eventually stop responding to my emails.

It took me a while to understand why, but eventually I realized that I was an amateur in a conversations with experts, trying to be a thought leader. Decisions at the city level are made years in advance and have a structured process to go from idea to reality. Many of the changes that I wanted to see are already being discussed at the city level, at least to some extent.

For me to engage productively with the planning for future transportation and development in the city, I needed to understand what was already in the pipeline.

3. The Challenge to Find Information about Upcoming Projects

For those of you who are familiar with the city of Richmond, you understand how information can sometimes feel like a precious commodity. The FOIA drama of late is bringing to the forefront just how difficult it is to navigate and to extract information from the city. I also think that the decline of print journalism such as the Richmond Times-Dispatch is exacerbating this problem.

Over the past year I’ve gotten more familiar with different ways to figure out what is planned for the city of Richmond. For example: I’m very excited about the hourly train service that will soon connect Richmond with DC and destinations beyond. Though the VPRA is doing a decent job posting timelines and work schedules, information about to the role of Main Street Station (RVM), or the short-term routing plan for expanded service are less readily available. I eventually was able to find the locally preferred alternatives in the final environmental impact statement, which include records of decisions made about the renovations planned for main street station, as well as the improvements needed to use RVM as a primary station to serve the city. I know now that Main Street Station will serve as a full service station in conjunction with the suburban Henrico Staples Mill Station, and that all trains will stop at both locations. Finding this information, however, was tedious and time consuming.

I started keeping a spreadsheet of these documents as well as information like the planned completion date of the project since I hit a point where I was interested in more projects than I could keep track of, and I was tired of “re-researching” deadlines and data that I had forgotten about. It only occurred to me recently that people may be interested in the contents of this spreadsheet, and would appreciate brief summaries of what is planned in the near and mid-term future in Richmond. I’m starting this substack to do just that.

4. The spreadsheet (and the future of this substack)

I think i’ve buried the headline thus far, so here’s the spreadsheet.

The spreadsheet orders each project that I’m currently interested in (that I’ve already researched) chronologically by completion date. Some dates are precise and others are slightly estimated by using different sources. When possible I’ll link the document or article where the information came from, though I have a preference for news articles over technical documents since they’re more accessible. You’ll notice that I’ll also link city maps, budgets, and technical documents such as engineering reports, records of decisions, and Environmental impact statements.

My plan for the next several posts is to feature projects on this list, share what I know about it, and talk about why I think it matters. The fall line trail, for example, is a well known and appreciated plan. I may actually need to explain, however, why I’m so excited about the CoStar Tower’s completion that it made it on to this list.

If you’d like to hear more about what’s coming soon in our city without needing to read and cross reference a plethora of technical documents and news stories, make sure to:

Subscribe now
